Part One

Safety evidence drifts as the design changes.

Medical devices became software-intensive systems. Their safety case is spread across documents that are traced but not always meaningful — and it loses alignment as the design evolves.

01
01 Device complexity

Medical devices are becoming complex.

Connected, configurable, software-defined cyber-physical systems. Safety now depends on how the whole system behaves, not on any single requirement.

As complexity accumulates,
how do we ensure safety under change?
Safety depends onbehaviornot only requirements text
Assumptions live ininterfacesnot only block diagrams
Risk controls crossteamssoftware · systems · clinical · V&V
Evidence must followchangeor it goes stale
Accumulating device complexity
increasing coupling
Clinical context · users, procedures, environment
Connected servicescloud · updates · telemetry · fleet data
Software behaviormodes · config · alarms · UI workflows
Cross-cuttingAI / automationinference · model drift · review burden
Device platformsensors · actuators · embedded control · hardware safety
So the question is: as complexity grows, how do we keep safety assured as the design keeps changing?
02 Fragmented evidence

The artifacts are linked, but the links lack meaning.

Specialized teams and a document-heavy process. Artifacts are linked, but the links often stop at IDs: they do not capture the design behavior being claimed, the architecture element that implements a control, or the conditions a test actually exercised.

Artifact island

Requirements

Traced to tests, but the link does not carry the safety claim it is meant to support.

User needsSystem reqsSoftware reqs
Architecture gap: the test is linked to a requirement, not to the behavior or design it verifies.
Artifact island

Risk

Hazards and controls live in separate files; controls are not anchored to the design.

HazardsHarmsControls
Architecture gap: the control is named, but not anchored to the design feature that implements it.
Artifact island

Verification

Evidence proves something — but not always the claim in today's released baseline.

TestsResultsDHF
Architecture gap: the test can pass without exercising the behavior that fails under load.
The problem isn't too few documents. It's that the links between them can't be checked for meaning or completeness.
03 Industry context

Safety-critical domains lean on architecture.

Aerospace and automotive treat architecture as the backbone of the safety case, and they write that discipline into their standards. Medical has strong standards too, but less of the architecture model.

Architecture-led

Aerospace

Architecture & allocation chains tie function, safety analysis, and verification evidence together.

ARP4754AARP4761DO-178C
Platform-led

Automotive

Platforms & contracts standardize safety mechanisms, interfaces, and reuse across product lines.

ISO 26262AUTOSARISO 21434
Process-led

Medical devices

Strong process, risk, electrical safety, and cybersecurity standards — but architecture maturity still varies.

ISO 14971IEC 62304IEC 60601IEC 81001-5-1ISO 13485
IEC 62304 requires software architecture, but it does not provide a shared model connecting system design, risk controls, cybersecurity, and verification evidence.
04 The gap

Why medical architecture stays weak.

The standards ask for architecture, risk, cybersecurity, and verification. The gap is one shared model that all of those activities can use.

Cross-functional handoffs Architecture is split across teams

Systems, software, risk, cyber, V&V, clinical, and quality each hold one slice.

Document-heavy QMS Evidence becomes the system of record

The DHF is reviewable, but design meaning is scattered across files.

Startup inheritance Code-first products get acquired

Architecture often lives in code, habits, and the people who built it.

MBSE tool cliff Tools exist, but setup is expensive

Licenses, method, training, governance, and migration delay value.

The result Architecture becomes a picture, not a computable contract.

It explains intent, but cannot answer the questions teams need during change.

Risk controls floatnot tied to design features
Cyber is separatenot tied to behavior
Tests miss behaviorwrong path, wrong load
Impact is manualdepends on expert memory
What is missing: an affordable architecture-centered model that ties design behavior, risk, cyber, V&V, and evidence together.
05 The answer

Put architecture at the core.

Make the architecture the computable center: intent, risk, requirements, behavior, verification, and evidence all connect through it — and stay checkable as the design changes.

Living modelArchitectureresponsibilities · interfaces · behavior · impact
IntentUse & assumptions
RiskHazards & controls
NeedRequirements
BehaviorFlows & modes
V&VVerification
ProofEvidence
This is what meMO implements: an architecture-centered model where the whole chain is typed and checkable.
Part Two

Introducing meMO.

meMO — said “memo” — is the Medical Engineering Modeling Ontology: four layers you can adopt independently — an ontology, a methodology, a toolchain, and a visual architect.

02
06 The stack

Four layers, adopt what you need.

meMO is a stack, not a single tool. You can start at any level — from a plain text model up to a visual review app. The next four slides take each layer in turn.

Layer 01 · Ontology

Ontology

Typed SysML v2 elements and links for hazards, controls, requirements, and evidence.

Defines what each element means.
Layer 02 · Methodology

Methodology

Predefined viewpoints, rules, workflow stages, and review gates.

A working structure to start from.
Layer 03 · Tools

Tools

Parser, validator, and CLI that check the model and generate documents.

Runs in CI like a build.
Layer 04 · Architect

Architect

A web app for diagrams, traceability, DSM, and DHF review.

Review without editing files.
Start with the layer that's useful to you now, and add the others later. The model underneath stays the same.

Ontology — a typed medical vocabulary.

A minimal, medically grounded SysML v2 vocabulary, published as an open spec in one memo:: namespace, version 0.2.0.

Typed elements

Every safety-relevant thing is a typed part with regulator-relevant attributes.

Intended UseHazardHarmRiskControlRequirementArchitectureBehaviorVerificationCaseEvidence
Typed links & rules
  • Semantic links carry roles, not free-form arrows.
  • Closure rules (CR-MED-*) traced to ISO 14971 and IEC 62304.
  • 18 architecture layers, with risk and cybersecurity as peers.
The next act walks the ontology layer by layer — each layer's definitions, then real instances from a worked example.
08 meMO · Methodology
01Ontology
02Methodology
03Tools
04Architect

Methodology — a starting structure.

So teams start from a working structure rather than an empty model: resolve scope to the device's safety class, use default viewpoints, apply usage rules, and bind the method to a project.

Risk-proportionate scope

ResolvedMethodology keys scope to SafetyClassKind (A/B/C) and lifecycle stage — not a rigor dial.

Viewpoints (ISO 42010)

Viewpoints per audience and workflow stage; a View binds that intent to content.

Rules & gates

ElementUsageRule / RelationUsageRule carry a RuleStrengthKind; WorkflowSteps and QualityGate exit criteria.

Project binding

ProjectMethodBinding pins a resolved method, with reusable ModelingPatterns and archetypes.

The methodology is editable and extendable — it guides how the ontology is applied without changing the ontology.

Tools — parse, check, generate.

A Turbo monorepo: a Langium-based core engine and a Commander CLI parse text-first models into a semantic graph and run the rules.

packages — core engine + CLI
packages/core
  parser · semantic graph · rule engine
  impact · DSM · DHF · importers

packages/cli   (memo)
  validate · dev · build · export · import
  ontology · dhf · ask · generate · req

$ cd examples/gpca-pump && memo dev
  → live model + validation at localhost
What the tools do
  • Parse text-first SysML v2 into a semantic graph.
  • Run native KerML closure & consistency checks — errors, warnings, completeness.
  • Import / export: Enterprise Architect, Cameo, OWL, CSV.
  • Generate DHF artifacts; validate in CI before review or release.
Run memo validate in CI, and each change produces a defined re-review scope.

Part Three

Walk the ontology, layer by layer.

One namespace, its layers, and — for each layer — the definitions and then real instances from GPCA, a public-domain infusion pump (IEC 62304 Class C).

03
11 Package shape

One namespace, one release: memo::

The ontology ships as a single SysML v2 package — memo::medical_device_library, version 0.2.0. Each sub-package is a focused library.

medical_device_library.sysml
package memo {
 package medical_device_library {
  public import memo::core::*;          // bases, enums, links
  public import memo::architecture::*;  // 18 layers
  public import memo::methodology::*;
  public import memo::viewpoints::*;
  public import memo::views::*;
  public import memo::compliance::*;
 }
}
C
memo::core · bases · enums · semantic links
A
memo::architecture · 18 ontology layers
M
memo::methodology · profiles · rules · gates
K
memo::compliance · artifacts · document views
Viewpoints, methodology, and compliance all build on the ontology rather than copying it.

13 Layer · Requirements
Context›Requirements›Functions›Behavior›Structure›Risk›Security›Verification

Requirements — needs become typed obligations.

Definitions on the left; the same kinds instantiated in GPCA on the right. Requirements are SysML v2 requirement defs, not docstring fields.

architecture/memo_requirements.sysml — definitions
requirement def StakeholderNeed :> RequirementDriver;
requirement def Requirement :> VerifiableElement {
  attribute statement       : String;
  attribute sourceKind      : RequirementSourceKind;
  attribute acceptanceCriteria : String;
}
requirement def SoftwareRequirement :> Requirement {
  attribute safetyClass : SafetyClassKind;
}
examples/gpca — instances
requirement needSafeTherapy : StakeholderNeed {
  attribute id = "NEED-001";
  attribute statement =
    "Support safe patient-controlled therapy.";
}
requirement reqLockout : SoftwareRequirement {
  attribute id = "REQ-025";
  attribute sourceKind = RequirementSourceKind::risk;
  attribute safetyClass = SafetyClassKind::C;
}
Same kinds, real values: REQ-025 carries its source (risk) and safety class as typed attributes you can query.
14 Layer · Risk & safety
Context›Requirements›Functions›Behavior›Structure›Risk›Security›Verification

Risk — hazard, control, residual.

The ISO 14971 chain as typed items. Cybersecurity is a peer layer: Threat :> RiskDriver, driving the same machinery as risk.

architecture/memo_risk.sysml — definitions
item def Hazard :> TraceableElement {
  attribute hazardType  : HazardTypeKind;
  attribute severity    : CriticalityKind;
  attribute foreseeable : Boolean;
}
item def RiskControl :> VerifiableElement {
  attribute controlKind        : RiskControlKind;
  attribute implementationKind : RiskControlImplementationKind;
}
part def RiskAfterMitigation :> Risk {
  attribute residualAcceptability : String;
}
examples/gpca — instances
part overdoseHazard : Hazard {
  attribute id = "HZ-001";
  attribute hazardType = HazardTypeKind::drugDeliveryError;
  attribute severity   = CriticalityKind::catastrophic;
}
part lockoutControl : RiskControl {
  attribute id = "RC-001";
  attribute controlKind = RiskControlKind::inherentSafeDesign;
  attribute implementationKind = RiskControlImplementationKind::softwareDesign;
}
Safety and security are peers — both feed the same RequirementDriver / VerifiableElement contract downstream.
15 Layer · Assurance
Context›Requirements›Functions›Behavior›Structure›Risk›Security›Verification

Assurance — cases, tests, evidence.

The verification layer closes the thread: a case with acceptance criteria, a test artifact, and evidence tied to a baseline.

architecture/memo_assurance.sysml — definitions
part def VerificationCase :> VerifiableElement {
  attribute methodKind        : VerificationMethodKind;
  attribute acceptanceCriteria : String;
}
part def TestArtifact :> EvidenceElement;
part def Evidence :> EvidenceElement {
  attribute evidenceType    : String;
  attribute integrityStatus : String;
}
examples/gpca — instances
part vcLockout : VerificationCase {
  attribute id = "VER-002";
  attribute methodKind = VerificationMethodKind::test;
  attribute acceptanceCriteria =
    "No bolus when lockout / max bolus active.";
}
part evidenceLockout : Evidence {
  attribute id = "EVD-001";
  attribute evidenceType = "verification evidence";
}
Acceptance criteria are a typed attribute — the rule engine can check that every high-severity control reaches an Evidence node.
16 Connecting the layers

Typed links connect the layers.

Layers don't connect by free-form arrows. Every relation is a native SysML v2 connection def specializing SemanticLink — its name is the verb, its typed ends carry the roles, a linkStatus carries state, and navigation is bidirectional.

DomainConnection kinds
RequirementDerivesFrom · SatisfiedBy · DerivesInto
FunctionAllocatedTo — function ↔ allocated element
InterfaceRealizesInterface · CrossesTrustBoundary · BindsToInterface
VerificationVerifiedBy · ProducesEvidence · Validates · IncludedIn
RiskMitigatesHazard · TracesRisk · AssessedAgainst
CyberThreatenedBy · Exploits · MitigatesVulnerability · ImpactsSafety
Because traceability is stored as data rather than a spreadsheet, the RMF view, V&V matrix, and impact analysis all read the same SemanticLink connections.
17 Compile the argument

We compile code. We should compile the safety argument.

With everything typed and linked, review questions become executable checks — native KerML closure constraints traced to ISO 14971, IEC 62304, and ISO 13485.

terminal — closure & consistency
$ memo validate

CR-MED-001  Hazard must have ≥1 risk control   (ISO 14971)
            Missing mitigation: hazAirInLine

CR-MED-003  Risk control must be verified      (ISO 14971 §7.4)
            Missing verification: rcDoorOpenAlarm

CR-MED-004  Pre-mitigation risk must be assessed
            against a risk matrix             (ISO 14971)

Result: 2 errors · 1 warning · thread HZ-001 closed
Why it matters
  • Find gaps before design review or audit.
  • Make closure visible to software, systems, risk, and V&V at once.
  • Run the rules in CI before merge or release.
  • Turn each change into a deterministic re-review scope.
That makes compliance a build step — something engineers can run and check.

19 Extension

Extend through methodology profiles.

Resolve scope, pick viewpoints, author usage rules, bind to a project, add your own domain kinds. The core ontology stays unchanged.

1
Resolve scope · ResolvedMethodology · safetyClassification = C · lifecycleStage = development
2
Pick viewpoints · Viewpoint · audience = safetyEngineer · stage = risk
3
Author rules · ElementUsageRule · elementTypeName = "Hazard" · strength = required
4
Bind to project · ProjectMethodBinding · projectName = "GPCA"
5
Add domain kinds · part def InfusionMode :> ModeState { … } in your own package
The rule: add packages and methodology profiles — don't edit core.
